documents.title: Drafting a generative AI-use policy for your course
tiers: Sample #3: limited use with attribution (AI encouraged, code conditions)
documents.summary: A Teaching and Learning Center guide for UCSC instructors on writing a course AI policy: required components, conditions on detection tools, four sample syllabus policies from restrictive to substantial use, and strategies for reducing misuse. It sets no university-wide stance.
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'it's important that you include a clear AI-use policy in your syllabus' and that the policy should align with 'your discipline, your department, and your course', then offers four sample policies from highly restrictive to substantial use. It hands the decision to instructors, so it delegates.

units.why: Tells instructors a syllabus AI policy is needed whether or not they use AI: 'it's important that you include a clear AI-use policy in your syllabus'. Instructor-directed, pre-course, a recommendation, so P09.
units.anchor: it’s important that you include a clear AI-use policy in your syllabus

units.why: Gives the reason for a syllabus policy: without one 'your students won't know what is expected'. It explains why the statement is needed, so P09 rather than P66 (which is about explaining the rules themselves).
units.anchor: your students won’t know what is expected, what is allowed, and what is prohibited
units.fit_note: Gives the reason for having a syllabus policy rather than the requirement itself.

units.why: Cites survey evidence that 'Students desire clarity' on allowed AI uses. Evidence is cited, so P55, though about student preferences and not learning.
units.anchor: Students desire clarity from you on the ethical and allowable uses
units.fit_note: Evidence concerns student preferences for clarity, not AI's effect on learning.

units.why: Recommends a policy aligned with 'the specific ethics and practices of your discipline, your department, and your course', leaving the content to the instructor within local norms, so P04.
units.anchor: aligns with the specific ethics and practices of your discipline, your department, and your course

units.why: Says to 'edit it in accordance with your expectations for your course' if sample language is used; adaptation is left to the instructor, so P04.
units.anchor: edit it in accordance with your expectations for your course
units.frag_start: If you do choose to incorporate
units.fit_note: Specifically instructs adapting provided template text.

units.why: States detection tools 'are neither accurate nor reliable' and 'should be used with caution'. Detector unreliability is P39, though use is not banned.
units.anchor: AI detection tools are neither accurate nor reliable
units.fit_note: Allows detectors with caution rather than rejecting them.

units.why: Sets conditions for detection software at UCSC: 'specific conditions that must be met' (local hosting, campus contract, or prior written student approval). This is a data-protection and vetting rule for tools, so P65 rather than P39.
units.anchor: there are specific conditions that must be met
units.frag_start: Additionally, at UC Santa Cruz, there
units.policy: At UC Santa Cruz, AI detection software may be used only if it is hosted locally with data protected from external access, contracted through campus purchasing, or approved in writing in advance by all of the instructor's students.
units.fit_note: Conditions on instructor use of detection software, not purchase approval in general.

units.why: Principle: 'Let your learning outcomes be your guide' for any choice to prevent, allow or require AI. Aligning AI decisions with objectives is P83.
units.anchor: Let your learning outcomes be your guide

units.why: Advises 'welcoming and inclusive language', first person, addressing students as 'you'. This is about wording of rules, so P66.
units.anchor: Use welcoming and inclusive language

units.why: Advises framing the policy as 'a commitment to helping students grow their capacities' rather than 'prohibitions and punitive measures'. Tone and framing of rules, P66.
units.anchor: rather than a list of prohibitions and punitive measures
units.frag_start: Frame your policy as a commitment

units.why: Says the message to students should reflect teaching philosophy, department priorities and field conventions; content is left to local context, P04.
units.anchor: should reflect your teaching philosophy, the priorities of your department, and the conventions of your

units.why: Predicts boundary-pushing and software change, then says 'Revisit and revise your policy each time you teach the course'. A review cycle, P54.
units.anchor: Revisit and revise your policy each time you teach the course
units.frag_start: Regardless of the approach you take

units.why: Asks instructors to state their personal and professional stance on AI and why, as a policy component; explaining reasons to students, P66.
units.anchor: What are your personal and professional stances on AI use? Why?
units.frag_start: What are your personal and professional
units.fit_note: Asks instructors to articulate their stance and reasons as a required component.

units.why: Lists task types (brainstorming, writing code, answering quiz questions...) that instructors must rule 'allowed or disallowed'. A menu of uses decided by the instructor, so P05 (categories of use).
units.anchor: For which of the following types of tasks will AI use be allowed or disallowed?
units.fit_note: A checklist of task categories to rule on, not named tiers.

units.why: Tells instructors to address exceptions such as Gemini summaries atop Google searches; routine embedded AI features, P100.
units.anchor: be sure to think through and address exceptions you’re willing to entertain
units.fit_note: Instructs instructors to decide on exceptions for embedded AI search summaries.

units.why: Instructors must tell students whether course materials may be uploaded to AI tools. P49 is nearest, but the document only requires stating a rule, so a fit note.

units.fit_note: Instructor must state a rule on uploading materials; it does not itself ban it.

units.why: Asks instructors to say which named tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Grammarly, predictive text) are allowed and on what conditions; covers built-in features too, so P07.
units.anchor: Which specific AI tools will be allowed or disallowed, and under what conditions?

notes: One included document: a teaching-center guide whose sample policies come from other UCSC courses (Sociology, a Python course, a hardware course). Sample-policy units are coded as the guide presents them (examples, not UCSC rules).
